description: Solo Kumasi participant building Earth Trends Observatory: a practical tool to explore NASA environmental measurements over time, compare regions, and inspect trends with uncertainty. The team is complete.
summary: Earth Trends Observatory helps people investigate how regional environmental measurements change over time. It turns authentic NASA POWER monthly temperature, rainfall, and humidity into transparent annual time series for 1981–2025. Users choose a region and period, compare actual levels or deviations from each location’s period mean, inspect the trend per decade with a 95% interval and significance test, and export reproducible evidence. Four bundled NASA snapshots keep the demonstration available without a live data request; custom coordinates and annual CSV import extend the investigation. Visible sources and limitations help students and data explorers question the evidence rather than mistake a fitted trend for a forecast.
details:
PROJECT DIRECTION

Project lead: William Osei Aborah, Kumasi, Ghana. William selected the practical Earth-trends goal, directed project review and presentation, and reviewed and approved the submitted work.

PURPOSE

Earth Trends Observatory combines regional time-series visualization and basic statistical analysis, directly addressing the Earth System Trend Detective challenge. It helps students, educators and environmental data explorers investigate what is changing, where, how fast, and with what uncertainty.

DATA AND WORKFLOW

Four authentic NASA POWER/MERRA-2 snapshots cover Accra, Ahmedabad, Manaus and Longyearbyen for 1981–2025. Users choose temperature, precipitation or relative humidity and a time window, then compare another region. Custom coordinates retrieve NASA data directly. Annual CSV import stays in the browser and requires units and provenance.

CSV and JSON evidence exports preserve observations, processing, sources, assumptions and contribution metadata. View links reproduce bundled-data filters. Fixed snapshots, exact source URLs, retrieval timestamps and SHA-256 hashes make the examples traceable.

METHOD

Only complete years with 12 valid months enter NASA analyses. Temperature and humidity use day-weighted annual means. Precipitation multiplies monthly mean daily rates by calendar days and sums annual millimetres. Ordinary least squares uses actual years and reports change per decade, a 95% Student-t slope interval, a two-sided p-value and R². The chart shows annual values, the linear fit and a fitted-mean confidence band.

The method adapts regional time-series visualization, least-squares regression, R² and significance testing from challenge-listed Acker et al. (2009), NTRS 20090042747, Methods. Its single-predictor ANOVA F-test equals the two-sided slope t-test (F=t²). No SeaWiFS measurements are used; POWER is additional NASA data. Our annual aggregation uses day weights rather than the paper's monthly-anomaly method.

IMPLEMENTATION AND VALIDATION

The prototype uses HTML, CSS, SVG and JavaScript, with a separate numerical module and no runtime AI service. Twenty-eight automated checks validate statistical reference cases, CSV parsing, calendar aggregation, source payload preservation and all four raw hashes. Browser checks covered filters, regional comparison, a live NASA request, evidence download, negative-temperature CSV export/import, invalid-period export prevention, mobile layout and production loading. A seven-slide demo and complete source download accompany the application.

LIMITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The design puts sources, uncertainty and clear explanations beside each result, supporting a reproducible first inspection of regional changes. This is an independent prototype; no NASA adoption, field deployment or operational validation is claimed.

MERRA-2 combines observations and models on an approximately 0.5° latitude by 0.625° longitude grid; it is not a city weather station. OLS inference assumes a linear trend, independent errors and constant variance, with approximately normal residuals for small samples. Serial correlation, multiple comparisons and measurement/model uncertainty are not corrected. The chart band is for the fitted mean, not future observations. Separate regional slope tests do not establish a significant difference between slopes. Trends do not establish causes or forecast conditions, and a non-significant result does not prove no change.

VERSION 1.1 IMPROVEMENTS

The chart now offers actual values or deviations from each region’s own selected-period mean. Centering makes change patterns easier to compare when regional averages differ; it preserves units and leaves slopes, p-values and confidence intervals unchanged. Shared views and JSON evidence record the display mode and baseline values, while CSV exports retain actual observations.

A descriptive adjacent-year residual correlation helps users notice time dependence. It is not an independence test or a correction to OLS inference. Seven additional numerical checks bring the passing local total to 28. The public GitHub repository includes the source, demo materials, licenses, contribution guidance and a test workflow for future development.

REFLECTIONS AND NEXT STEPS

Developing this prototype reinforced that a useful environmental chart must preserve the reasoning behind it. Complete-year coverage and calendar-day weighting matter because temperature means and precipitation rates require different aggregation. Comparing regions also exposed a presentation problem: large differences in average conditions can obscure changes over time. The added deviation-from-period-mean view addresses that display issue while retaining raw observations and unchanged trend statistics. A descriptive residual-correlation readout makes another limitation easier to notice: time dependence can affect ordinary least-squares uncertainty. Provenance, downloadable evidence and explicit assumptions support reproducible exploration, but software checks are not field validation. The next stage is scientific review of correlation-aware inference, broader spatial coverage and evaluation with intended users before making operational claims. These remain future steps rather than completed outcomes.

AI assistance: research, code, analysis, writing, design and slides; details in project credits.
